JSON: Name: ai_biosensor_arts_amr Title: Integration of portable biosensor-based real-time detection, AI-driven antimicrobial-resistance prediction, and community co-designed arts engagement to reduce inappropriate outpatient antibiotic prescribing and improve local AMR hotspot detection Short Hypothesis: Integrating portable biosensor-based real-time microbial detection with AI-driven resistance prediction and community co-designed arts engagement will reduce inappropriate outpatient antibiotic prescriptions by at least 20% and increase early detection sensitivity of local antimicrobial-resistance hotspots relative to standard stewardship and surveillance over 12 months. Related Work: Portable biosensors (electrochemical, fluorescence, SPR, paper-based assays) have been developed for rapid pathogen detection but often lack real-world field validation and high-throughput integration with clinical workflows. AI and machine-learning models have been applied to genomic and clinical datasets to predict resistance phenotypes and prioritize antimicrobial candidates, yet these models are commonly trained on biased surveillance or culture collections and show limited external generalizability. Public engagement and behavioral interventions (including arts-based campaigns) have improved awareness and self-reported stewardship outcomes but rarely demonstrate changes in prescribing or diagnostic uptake. Existing interventions typically address either technical surveillance (biosensors/AI) or social-behavioral change (education/arts) in isolation. Limitations across prior work include fragmented data standards and interoperability, absence of randomized controlled evaluations that link community engagement to measurable clinical outcomes, limited validation of sensor-derived resistance signals against culture/WGS references in community settings, and scarce evidence on combined effect sizes when technical surveillance is paired with community-driven stewardship. Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) requires coordinated technical surveillance and community-level behavioral change. We propose an integrated research pipeline that combines portable biosensor detection, AI-driven resistance prediction, and community co-designed arts engagement to reduce inappropriate outpatient antibiotic use and improve early detection of local resistance hotspots. The pipeline deploys low-cost point-of-care biosensors in primary-care clinics and community sites, streams sensor outputs to an AI model that predicts resistance signatures in near real-time, and couples these technical outputs with arts-informed engagement co-created with local stakeholders to reshape prescribing expectations. The principal contribution is a quantified evaluation of the combined technical and social intervention using a cluster-randomized controlled design, with paired microbiological reference testing and clinical prescribing outcomes. Expected outcomes include a measurable reduction in inappropriate prescriptions, improved sensitivity and timeliness of local AMR detection, and evidence on the marginal contribution of arts-informed engagement versus surveillance alone. This work will produce interoperable datasets, open AI models, and protocols for combined technical-social AMR interventions. Experiments: Design: cluster-randomized controlled trial (12-month intervention) across 40 primary-care clinic clusters in one region (randomized into four arms, n=10 clusters/arm): (A) standard stewardship (control), (B) biosensor + usual stewardship, (C) arts engagement + usual stewardship, (D) biosensor + AI + community co-designed arts engagement + stewardship. Datasets: (1) biosensor time-series outputs (sensor ID, timestamp, raw signal, processed concentration index), (2) clinical electronic medical record (EMR) logs (consultation ID, diagnosis code, antibiotic prescribed, dose, clinician ID), (3) reference microbiology (culture + minimum inhibitory concentration and whole-genome sequencing) on paired throat/urine/wound samples for a stratified 20% subsample of symptomatic patients, (4) patient/staff pre/post surveys (knowledge, attitudes, intended behaviour), (5) environmental swabs from clinic/community sites monthly, (6) cost and resource logs. Baselines: standard stewardship (A), biosensor-only (B), arts-only (C). Primary outcome: rate of inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions per 100 consultations (inappropriateness defined by local guideline algorithm applied to EMR diagnosis). Secondary outcomes: sensitivity, specificity, AUROC of biosensor+AI resistance prediction vs reference culture/WGS; median time-to-detection from sample to actionable result; change in knowledge/attitude scores; change in local resistance prevalence (culture/WGS) at 12 months; incremental cost per avoided inappropriate prescription. AI model training and validation: partition patient-level data by clinic with 70/15/15 training/validation/test splits at cluster level; use nested cross-validation and temporal holdout for prospective evaluation. Statistical analysis: mixed-effects negative binomial regression for prescription rates (cluster random intercepts), logistic/mixed models for binary outcomes; pre-specified alpha=0.05 with Bonferroni correction for primary/secondary families. Ablation studies: (1) compare arm B vs D to quantify marginal effect of arts engagement; (2) compare biosensor+raw-output (no AI) vs biosensor+AI to quantify AI contribution; (3) internal ablation of AI features (signal-only vs signal+clinical metadata vs signal+environmental data). Additional experiments: external validation on held-out clinics in a second region (n>=10), and sensitivity analysis varying biosensor detection thresholds and sampling proportions. Data governance: implement FAIR principles, trained models and pre-processing pipelines versioned and evaluated for calibration and fairness across demographic strata. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: biosensor drift, contamination, limited limit-of-detection for low-burden infections, high false-positive or false-negative rates under field conditions. AI risks: model overfitting to training clusters, bias from non-representative training data, concept drift over time, and opaque model decisions that reduce clinician trust. Data limitations: incomplete EMR data, sampling bias in culture/WGS subsample, non-random participation in surveys, and interoperability gaps between sensor, clinical, and laboratory datasets. Evaluation confounders: concurrent policy changes or unrelated stewardship campaigns may bias measured prescription changes; Hawthorne effect among clinicians. Scalability and compute: real-time AI inference at edge or low-bandwidth sites may be constrained by compute and connectivity; costs of sensors and maintenance limit scale-up. Regulatory and ethical constraints: approvals for diagnostic deployment may delay fieldwork and limit generalizability; community engagement outcomes may not be transferable across cultural contexts. Generalization limits: results from a single region and set of clinic types may not generalize to tertiary hospitals, veterinary settings, or different health systems. Sustainability: intervention effects may wane after study support ends; recurring costs and supply-chain dependencies for consumable sensors may hinder long-term adoption.
